sub: Named after its first word, ʿabasa: “he frowned”
theme: A gentle reproach teaching that a sincere seeker matters more than a proud leader, then a rebuke to ungrateful man and a warning about the Day of Judgement.
story: Revealed in Makkah, among the very earliest surahs. The Prophet ﷺ was speaking earnestly with leaders of Quraysh, hoping they would accept Islam. ʿAbdullāh ibn Umm Maktūm, a blind early Muslim, came and asked: “Teach me from what Allah has taught you.”

Unable to see that the Prophet ﷺ was busy, he kept calling out. The Prophet ﷺ disliked the interruption, frowned and turned back to the leaders. He was eager for their guidance and expected to teach this committed Muslim later. It was never contempt for the poor.

Allah revealed this surah as a gentle reproach and a lasting lesson. Afterwards the Prophet ﷺ honoured him, greeting him: “Welcome to the one about whom my Lord reproached me.” From ayah 17 the surah turns to the disbelievers.

sections.title: The Prophet ﷺ frowns at a blind seeker; Allah gently corrects him
sections.meaning: The Prophet ﷺ frowned and turned away when a blind man interrupted. Allah gently reminds him: this man might have grown purer or benefited from a reminder. The one who thinks he needs nothing got full attention, while the sincere seeker who came fearing Allah was overlooked.
points: He frowned and turned away when the blind man came
Perhaps he would be purified or benefit from the reminder
You attend to the self-satisfied; his refusal is not on you
The one who came eagerly, fearing Allah, you were distracted from
sections.matters: It sets a lasting rule for calling people to Allah: a sincere seeker, however weak or poor, deserves attention before a proud person who shows no interest. A certain benefit is never given up for a doubtful one.
sections.story: The Prophet ﷺ was speaking with Quraysh leaders, hoping they would believe. ʿAbdullāh ibn Umm Maktūm, who was blind, kept calling: “Teach me from what Allah has taught you.” The Prophet ﷺ frowned and turned away, and these ayat were revealed.
explained: ʿAbasa wa tawallā: he frowned and turned away. Allah speaks of the Prophet ﷺ in the third person here, out of respect, then turns to him warmly: how could you know? The blind man might have been purified, or at least taken a reminder that benefited him.

The one who istaghnā, who feels he needs nothing, gets your full attention, yet you are not to blame if he refuses to be purified. Your duty is only to convey. But the one who came hurrying, fearing Allah, is the one you were distracted from.
teaches: Every sincere seeker matters, even if weak, poor or unknown.
Status and wealth don’t make someone more worthy of your time.
Don’t give up a certain benefit for a doubtful one.
Excuse people who break etiquette without realising it.
Your job is to convey; guidance belongs to Allah.
sections.hook: Two “as for” lines face each other: ammā man istaghnā (5) and wa ammā man jāʾaka (8). Yazzakkā, “be purified”, appears twice, at 3 and 7.

sections.title: The Quran: a reminder for all, in honoured pages carried by angels
sections.meaning: No, it should not be so. These ayat are a reminder, and whoever wills will take heed. The Quran is kept in honoured, exalted and purified pages, in the hands of noble, obedient angels who carry it.
points: No! It is a reminder; whoever wills will remember it
In honoured pages, raised high and purified
Carried by noble, righteous angel-messengers
sections.matters: Section 1 showed who deserves attention. This one shows why: the message is honoured in heaven itself, so it does not depend on proud people accepting it. Whoever wills will take heed.
sections.story: No specific incident. It follows the blind man’s story directly: kallā tells the Prophet ﷺ not to repeat it, and “it” is either this surah or the whole Quran.
explained: Kallā: don’t do that again. Innahā tadhkirah: this advice, or the whole Quran, is a reminder for everyone, noble or poor alike. Whoever wills will remember it and act on it. No one is forced.

It is written in ṣuḥuf mukarramah, honoured pages, raised high in rank and purified, out of the reach of devils. They are in the hands of safarah: angels who carry the revelation like envoys, or who write it. They are kirām, noble, and bararah, obedient and righteous.
teaches: The Quran is honoured in heaven, so honour it here.
Guidance is offered to all, but no one is forced.
Whoever carries the Quran should strive to be noble and righteous.
Struggling with recitation still earns a double reward.
sections.hook: Three words describe the pages (mukarramah, marfūʿah, muṭahharah) and three describe their carriers (safarah, kirām, bararah). Tadhkirah (11) and dhakarahu (12) share one root.

sections.title: Ungrateful man, from a drop to grave and rising, still hasn’t obeyed
sections.meaning: Cursed is man, how ungrateful he is! Allah made him from a drop, shaped and measured him, eased his way, then gives him death and a grave, and will raise him when He wills. Yet man has still not done what he was commanded.
points: Cursed is man; how ungrateful he is
From what? A drop, then shaped in proportion
Then He eased the way for him
Death, a grave, and resurrection when Allah wills
No! He has not done what he was commanded
sections.matters: The rebuke now turns to the disbeliever himself. His whole life story, from a humble drop to the grave, is a favour from Allah and proof that He can bring him back.
sections.story: Mainly about every person who denies. Reportedly ayah 17 was revealed about ʿUtbah ibn Abī Lahab, who rejected Sūrat an-Najm.
explained: Qutila al-insān: may man be cursed, meaning the one who denies. Mā akfarah: how deep his ingratitude is! Think where he came from: a nuṭfah, a small drop. From it Allah created him and qaddarah: shaped him in proportion and decreed his lifespan, provision and deeds.

Then He eased his path: either his way out of his mother’s womb, or the way of right and wrong, made clear to him. Then He gives him death and honours him with a grave, and when He wills He raises him. Kallā: yet man still hasn’t done what Allah commanded.
teaches: Remember your humble beginning; it leaves no room for arrogance.
Every stage of life, even burial, is a favour from Allah.
The One who created you once can raise you again.
No one has fully done what Allah asked, so keep striving.
sections.hook: The life story moves in steps with thumma, “then”: He eased (20), He caused death (21), He resurrects (22). Kallā closes it (23), just as kallā opened section 2 (11).

sections.title: Let man study his food: rain, split earth, grain, fruit and pasture
sections.meaning: Man should reflect on his food. Allah pours down rain, splits the earth, and grows grain, grapes, fodder, olives, palms, thick gardens, fruit and pasture: provision for people and their animals. Dead earth coming to life also shows how the dead will rise.
points: Look at your food: rain poured, earth split open
Grain, grapes, fodder, olives and palms
Dense gardens, fruit and pasture
Provision for you and your livestock
sections.matters: Having reminded man of his own creation, the surah points to his daily food. Every meal is a chain of Allah’s favours, meant to produce gratitude, and a living proof of the resurrection.
sections.story: No specific incident. It continues the reply to ungrateful man by pointing to the food he eats every day.
explained: Falyanẓur: let man really look at his food and how it reaches him. Allah pours down rain in torrents, then splits the earth with new shoots. From it He grows ḥabb, every kind of grain, then grapes, qaḍb (fresh green fodder), olives and date palms.

Ḥadāʾiq ghulbā are gardens thick with tall, tangled trees. Fākihah is fruit for people, and abb is pasture for animals. All of it is matāʿ, provision for you and your livestock. Whoever reflects on this is moved to thank his Lord and obey Him.
teaches: Every meal is a chain of blessings; eat with gratitude.
Life from dead earth is a picture of resurrection.
Allah provides for your animals as well as for you.
Say “I don’t know” rather than guess about the Quran.
sections.hook: The food list runs in pairs joined by wa: grapes and fodder (28), olives and palms (29), fruit and pasture (31). It ends like An-Nāziʿāt 79:33: matāʿan lakum wa li-anʿāmikum.

sections.title: The Deafening Blast: each flees his family, then faces shine or darken
sections.meaning: When aṣ-ṣākhkhah, the deafening blast, comes, a man runs from his brother, mother, father, wife and children, each too busy with himself. Then faces split in two: some bright, laughing and joyful; others dusty and darkened. Those are the disbelievers, the wicked.
points: The Deafening Blast arrives
A man flees brother, mother, father, wife and children
Everyone has worry enough of his own
Some faces bright, laughing, rejoicing
Others dusty and darkened: the disbelieving, wicked ones
sections.matters: The surah ends where it was heading: the Day of Judgement. Those who turned away in arrogance and those who came humbly seeking will be sorted by faith and deeds, not by status.
sections.story: No specific incident. It closes the warning to the disbelievers who rejected the message.
explained: Aṣ-ṣākhkhah is the blast that almost deafens the ears, the blowing of the Trumpet. On that Day a man sees his brother, mother, father, wife and children, and runs from them. The terror is so great that each person is fully taken up with himself.

When the Prophet ﷺ said people will be gathered unclothed, he was asked if they would look at each other. He answered: every man that Day will have enough to occupy him. Then faces divide: bright and laughing with good news, or dust-covered and dark. Those are al-kafarah al-fajarah.
teaches: No relationship can save you on that Day; only your deeds.
Build your worth with Allah, not with people.
What is in the heart will show on the face.
Disbelief in the heart and wickedness in action go together.
sections.hook: The surah opens with a frown (ʿabasa) and closes with faces: wujūhun yawmaʾidhin starts both 38 and 40. The fleeing list runs brother → mother and father → wife and children.

groups.text: The Prophet ﷺ frowned and turned away because the blind man came to him.
How could you know? He might have been purified, or taken a reminder that helped him.
You attend to the one who feels no need, though you’re not to blame if he stays unpurified.
But the one who came eagerly, fearing Allah, you were distracted from.
No! This is a reminder, and whoever wills will remember it.
It is in honoured pages, raised high and kept pure.
Carried by the hands of noble, righteous angels.
Cursed is ungrateful man. Allah made him from a drop and shaped him in proportion.
Then He eased his way, gave him death and a grave, and will raise him when He wills.
No! Man has still not done what Allah commanded him.
Let man look at his food: rain poured down, earth split open.
Allah grows grain, grapes, green fodder, olives and date palms.
Dense gardens, fruit and pasture: provision for you and your animals.
When the Blast comes, a man flees his brother, parents, wife and children, each busy with himself.
Some faces that Day are bright, laughing and full of joy.
Others are dusty and covered in darkness: the disbelieving, wicked ones.

1.explain: ʿAbasa: frowned. Tawallā: turned away. It speaks of the Prophet ﷺ in the third person, as if about someone else, out of respect, sparing him a direct rebuke.
1.why: The Prophet ﷺ was talking with Quraysh leaders, hoping they would accept Islam. ʿAbdullāh ibn Umm Maktūm, who was blind, came asking to be taught and kept calling out. The Prophet ﷺ frowned and turned away from him.

2.explain: Because al-aʿmā, the blind man, came. Calling him “blind” also excuses him: he could not see that the Prophet ﷺ was busy with others.

3.explain: Now Allah addresses him directly and gently: what would make you know? Yazzakkā: perhaps he would be purified by what he learned from you.

4.explain: Or yadhdhakkaru: he would take the reminder to heart and it would benefit him. At the least, his remembrance and fear of Allah would grow.

5.explain: Istaghnā: he thinks he has no need of Allah or of faith, because of his wealth.

6.explain: Taṣaddā: you turn toward him and give him your full attention, hoping he will be guided.

7.explain: You are not to blame if he does not purify himself. Your duty is only to convey the message.

8.explain: Yasʿā: he came to you hurrying, eager to be guided by what you would say.

9.explain: Wa huwa yakhshā: and he fears Allah. That fear is what brought him to you.

10.explain: Talahhā: you were busy with others and distracted from him. A seeker’s certain benefit should not be set aside for an uncertain hope.

11.explain: Kallā: don’t do that again. Innahā tadhkirah: this surah, or the Quran as a whole, is a reminder for all people alike.

12.explain: Fa man shāʾa dhakarah: whoever wills will remember it and act on it. The choice is laid before everyone.

13.explain: Fī ṣuḥufin mukarramah: it is written in pages honoured by Allah, either the Preserved Tablet or the scriptures of the prophets.

14.explain: Marfūʿah: raised high in rank. Muṭahharah: purified, free of any addition or loss, and out of the reach of devils.

15.explain: Bi-aydī safarah: in the hands of angels who carry the revelation like envoys between Allah and His messengers, or who write it down.

16.explain: Kirām: noble. Bararah: obedient and righteous. The Prophet ﷺ said the skilled reciter will be with these angels, and the one who struggles to recite gets a double reward.

17.explain: Qutila al-insān: may man be cursed, meaning the one who denies. Mā akfarah: how intense his ingratitude is, despite all Allah has given him.
17.why: Reportedly revealed about ʿUtbah ibn Abī Lahab, who had accepted Islam, then turned back when Sūrat an-Najm came, saying he believed in all the Quran except that surah.

18.explain: From what did He create him? The question points to something so humble it leaves no room for pride.

19.explain: From a nuṭfah, a drop. Qaddarah: He shaped him in proportion, stage by stage, and decreed his lifespan, provision, deeds, and whether he would end happy or miserable.

20.explain: Thumma as-sabīla yassarah: then He eased his way, either out of his mother’s womb at birth, or along the path of right and wrong, made clear to him.

21.explain: Then He gives him death and aqbarah: provides him a grave, honouring him with burial instead of leaving him in the open like animals.

22.explain: Then, when He wills, ansharah: He brings him back to life for judgement. The One who began him can repeat it.

23.explain: Kallā: no! Lammā yaqḍi: man has still not done what Allah commanded him, despite all these favours.

24.explain: Falyanẓur: let man look closely at his food, how Allah planned it and brought it to him, and reflect.

25.explain: Annā ṣababnā al-māʾa ṣabbā: We poured down rain from the clouds in abundance.

26.explain: Then We split the earth open so new plants push through. Plants rising from lifeless earth are also a sign that decayed bodies can be raised.

27.explain: Fa anbatnā fīhā ḥabbā: We grew in it grain, every kind of seed people live on, like wheat and barley.

28.explain: ʿInab: grapes. Qaḍb: fresh green fodder, cut again and again for animals to eat.

29.explain: Zaytūn: olives, eaten and pressed for oil. Nakhl: date palms, whose fruit is eaten unripe, ripe and dried.

30.explain: Ḥadāʾiq ghulbā: gardens thick with tall, dense trees whose branches wrap around each other.

31.explain: Fākihah: fruit that people enjoy. Abb: pasture that animals graze. Asked about abb, Abu Bakr said he would never say anything about Allah’s Book without knowledge.

32.explain: Matāʿan lakum wa li-anʿāmikum: provision for you and your livestock. Reflecting on it should lead to thanks and obedience.

33.explain: Aṣ-ṣākhkhah: the deafening blast, so loud it nearly bursts the ears. Either a name for the Day of Judgement or the blowing of the Trumpet.

34.explain: Yafirru al-marʾ: a man runs from his own brother. He sees him and flees, because the terror is so great.

35.explain: …and from his mother and his father. Even the closest bonds bring no help that Day.

36.explain: …and from ṣāḥibatih, his wife, and his children. Even the greatest messengers will say “myself, myself” on that Day.

37.explain: Shaʾnun yughnīh: each person has worry enough to keep him from anyone else. The Prophet ﷺ recited this when asked if people, gathered unclothed, would look at each other.

38.explain: Wujūhun yawmaʾidhin musfirah: some faces that Day will be bright and shining. These are the people of Paradise.

39.explain: Ḍāḥikah mustabshirah: laughing and rejoicing at the good news of their safety and Allah’s honour.

40.explain: Other faces will have ghabarah on them: dust, and the gloom of grief.

41.explain: Tarhaquhā qatarah: darkness and blackness will cover them, faces that know their ruin.

42.explain: Al-kafarah al-fajarah: they combined disbelief in their hearts with wickedness in their actions.
